articles.title: Netanyahu defies exit polls as vote shifts in his favor, but majority remains elusive
articles.summary: With 70% of votes counted, Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud leads, but three possible paths to government formation keep Israel's election uncertain.
articles.body: TEL AVIV, Israel — Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's political bloc gained ground Wednesday morning as Israel counted votes from its first national election since the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas massacre, but remained short of the majority needed to form a government, leaving the country facing another potential political deadlock. With approximately 70% of votes counted, Netanyahu's right-wing and religious bloc stood at 54 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, compared with 47 for the main opposition and 19 for Arab parties, according to partial election results reported by Israeli media. Netanyahu's Likud led with 27 seats, while former Israeli military chief Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party held 20. As both Netanyahu and Eisenkot claimed victory Tuesday night, Israelis told Fox News Digital that although they had expected a tight race, the shifting numbers and uncertainty over who could form a government had left many confused about what comes next. ISRAEL HEADS INTO DEEPLY DIVIDED ELECTION AS OCT. 7 RECKONING LOOMS: WHAT TO KNOW Despite Netanyahu's lead, the parties outside his governing bloc collectively held 66 seats, a majority in the 120-seat Knesset, creating a potential path for the opposition to challenge his leadership if it can secure sufficient cooperation from Arab lawmakers. The results marked a shift from Tuesday night's initial exit polls, which prompted celebrations at Eisenkot's campaign headquarters in Tel Aviv. Eisenkot called on Netanyahu to accept the results and step aside, while Netanyahu declared later in the night from his headquarters in Jerusalem that Likud had emerged as the country's largest party and urged the formation of a strong right-wing government. The election has now shifted from the ballot box to a potentially complicated battle over coalition-building. President Donald Trump took credit Wednesday morning for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's stronger-than-expected election performance, suggesting his endorsement helped shift the momentum of the race. NETANYAHU FIGHTS FOR POLITICAL FUTURE AS ISRAEL HEADS TO POLLS WITH IRAN THREAT LOOMING In a post on Truth Social, Trump shared a statement from Irving C. Schwartz, who wrote, "When President Trump endorsed Bibi Netanyahu, the whole tide turned, and now, rather than a decisive defeat for a Great Prime Minister, it looks like a big come-from-behind stalemate, or even a WIN for Netanyahu." Later, speaking to reporters near Air Force One, Trump said, "I heard the poll numbers were wrong ... the exit polls; I heard he [Netanyahu] did very well. It was pretty close, but very well. When the endorsement went out, it helped him a lot." "It's a little bit early, but I'm hearing in Israel, top people say, 'Wow! He did a lot better than people thought.' It's looking like maybe a stalemate or a win," Trump added. JD VANCE DECLINES TO ENDORSE NETANYAHU DESPITE TRUMP'S STRONG BACKING Arab parties could hold the key The growing influence of Arab parties has emerged as one of the most consequential factors in determining Israel's next government. According to the partial results, the Joint List held 13 seats and Ra'am, led by Mansour Abbas, held six, giving Arab parties a combined 19 seats. Abbas signaled openness to political negotiations, saying figures from both sides of Israel's political divide had approached him. "Everyone is talking to us, not just the change bloc," Abbas told Israel's Channel 12. Democrats leader Yair Golan went further, openly calling for the formation of a new government in cooperation with Arab parties. "Netanyahu lost. I know how to count to 120–65 is greater than 55. That's how Israeli democracy works. Period," Golan wrote on X. Golan also rejected Netanyahu's distinction between Jewish and Arab political support, arguing that every Israeli citizen's vote should carry equal weight. "The vote of an Israeli citizen in Tira is worth exactly the same as the vote of an Israeli citizen in Givat Shmuel," he wrote. Golan's figures reflected an earlier stage of the count, but his argument highlighted an emerging disagreement within the opposition over whether to include Arab parties in the next government. Eisenkot has previously expressed opposition to including Ra'am in his coalition, while Netanyahu has warned against any government dependent on Arab parties. BENJAMIN NETANYAHU'S LEGACY AND POLITICAL FUTURE ON THE LINE IN ISRAEL'S OCT 27 ELECTION Three possible paths to forming a government Netanyahu could attempt to expand his current coalition by winning support from at least seven lawmakers outside his right-wing and religious bloc, which would bring him to the 61 seats needed for a conventional parliamentary majority. Alternatively, Eisenkot could seek enough parliamentary recommendations, potentially including those of Arab parties, to persuade President Isaac Herzog to give him the first opportunity to form a government. Those recommendations would not necessarily require Arab parties to join a future coalition. However, Eisenkot would still need enough parliamentary support to secure a confidence vote. A third possibility is another deadlock, with neither leader able to form a government and Israel potentially facing another election. The final outcome remains uncertain as vote counting continues, including ballots cast by soldiers and other voters using special voting procedures. Official results are scheduled for Nov. 4, after which Herzog will consult with parliamentary factions and select a lawmaker to attempt to form the next government. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP That candidate will initially have 28 days to negotiate coalition agreements, with the possibility of a 14-day extension. Until a new government takes office, Netanyahu will remain prime minister.

articles.title: Serbian shot dead after attacking officer outside Israeli embassy, minister says
articles.summary: Authorities say the attacker in Belgrade was an underage male who was being monitored by security services.
articles.body:
Serbian police shot dead a young man outside the Israeli embassy in Belgrade in the early hours of Wednesday after what authorities called a "terrorist attack".

The country's interior minister, Ivica Dacic, said the attacker had rushed at a police officer with two knives while shouting the phrase "Allahu Akbar". The officer sustained a minor knife wound to the face and shot the attacker.

Dacic said the suspect has not been identified, but he was a minor and Serbian citizen who was being monitored by security services as he was "known to be a supporter of the Islamic State".

Speaking to reporters outside the embassy, Dacic said an investigation is ongoing, but security services said the suspect had posted a picture of the Islamic State flag on his Instagram.

Dacic raised the country's terrorism threat level to "red alert" - the highest threat level – meaning stricter security checks and increased police presence at places like infrastructure facilities and areas where large crowds gather.

The interior minister said he had visited the injured police officer, who was reportedly doing well and did not need hospital care for his wounds.

Armed security personnel were seen standing guard outside the Israeli embassy on Wednesday morning.

Israel's foreign ministry confirmed in a social media post that no embassy personnel were injured and the mission was closed at the time of the incident.

This is the second such attack on Belgrade's Israeli embassy in less than three years; in June 2024, a man shot a police officer in the neck with a crossbow.

The officer who was shot survived the attack and shot dead the assailant, identified as a Serbian man who had converted to Islam.

Wednesday's attack comes just one day after elections in Israel.

articles.title: Tanzania celebrates first natural gas discovery in more than 10 years
articles.summary: The energy minister described it as a "major milestone" for the East African nation.
articles.body:
Tanzania has announced a significant discovery of natural gas in the Mnazi Bay area in the south of the country - the first such find in a decade.

Energy Minister Juma Homera attended a ceremony at the Kasa-1X ST2 well, which is jointly owned by state-owned Tanzania Petroleum Development Corporation (TPDC) and French oil firm Maurel & Prom, to mark the occasion.

He said the estimated 223 billion cubic feet (6.3 billion cubic metres) discovery was a "major milestone" in the development of the small oil and gas sector in the East African nation.

The new well is expected to start production early next month and is intended to boost domestic supplies.

Tanzania has existing natural gas reserves of 57.54 trillion cubic feet.

"The discovery is important in ensuring the country has reliable, clean and safe energy at affordable costs, particularly at a time when demand is increasing due to industrial growth and other economic activities," Homera said.

Natural gas accounted for nearly 80% of Tanzania's sources of electricity generation, according to government statistics for 2024.

In recent years, the country has also encouraged the use of compressed natural gas to power vehicles, with natural gas plants and filling stations set up mostly in the largest city, Dar es Salaam.

Some Tanzanians have been converting their vehicles to a dual-fuel system - with the locally available natural gas allowing for cheaper prices than petrol.

Tanzania made its first natural gas discovery in 1974 on the Songo Songo Island in the south-east Lindi region, followed by a second discovery at Mnazi Bay in neighbouring region of Mtwara in 1982.

The commercialisation of these discoveries began in 2004. This propelled further gas exploration both onshore and offshore, with the largest single discovery of 2.7 trillion cubic feet of natural gas in 2016.

articles.title: Norway and Finland hold rare phone call with Putin: What that means
articles.summary: The two Nordic leaders are attempting to influence US-brokered talks in Abu Dhabi to end the war in Ukraine.
articles.body:
The leaders of Norway and Finland have held a rare call with Russian President Vladimir Putin to push for an end to the war in Ukraine, ahead of a planned round of United States-brokered talks in Abu Dhabi next month.

The call on Tuesday marked a break from a longstanding policy among Western European heads of state to avoid direct talks with the Russian leader.

Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Stoere spoke with Putin for 90 minutes.

US President Donald Trump told reporters on Tuesday that direct talks between the Russian and Ukrainian presidents would happen “very soon”. But with Trump increasingly siding with Putin over Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Western leaders have been largely sidelined from US-led negotiations to end the Ukraine war.

Gerhard Mangott, an Austrian political analyst, said European governments had “manoeuvred themselves into a dead end” when it came to finding a solution to the war, and Tuesday’s call was an effort to establish a channel for dialogue.

The Nordic leaders are hoping to influence the diplomatic process, following a policy shift by US President Donald Trump in favour of Russia. US ties with Ukraine have sunk to their lowest point in 18 months since Trump blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy facilities for the rise in the cost of diesel, which has doubled in the US this year.

Trump struck a deal with Putin to release Russian diesel stocks to the US and global markets despite sanctions on Russian oil. He also waived newly approved US sanctions on Russia, causing anger in Europe and within his Republican Party, which had largely supported them.

Ukraine also accused the US of restricting its access to Starshield, the military-grade Starlink satellite system that provides missile guidance intelligence.

Stubb described the discussion with Putin as “frank and substantive”.

“We are neighbouring countries to Russia. The outcome of this war will have a direct impact on our and the broader European security. Ending the war requires direct discussions,” the Finnish president said.

Stoere said he and Stubb had “stressed the importance of de-escalation” to Putin.

In a post on X, Stubb said the call “was a follow-up to the meeting in Oslo on 20 October”, referring to talks between US special envoy Steve Witkoff and Zelenskyy, held amid deteriorating relations between Washington and Kyiv. Stubb said the conversation with Putin was prepared “in consultation with Ukraine and the United States .

Stubb stressed that the joint call was held in individual capacities as leaders of Norway and Finland, not as representatives of Europe.

“We emphasised that our support for Ukraine remains unwavering,” Stubb said.

Stubb said all Western allies were consulted on the initiative, and that Ukraine had sought the opening of a new channel of communication, arguing that Europe could not contribute to peace efforts by giving Russia “the silent treatment”.

Norway’s Prime Minister Stoere added: “Talking to the other side does in no way mean that we take off the pressure. So I believe that that is something Europe also should do with voices that can be understood on that side.”

The conversation with Putin was followed up with a call to Zelenskyy.

The Kremlin’s summary of the conversation suggests the Russian president maintained a hard line.

“It was emphasised that achieving a just and long-term peace is possible only if the legitimate interests of the Russian Federation are fully and unconditionally taken into account,” it said.

The Kremlin also made reference to “the confrontational policies of EU and NATO countries, which are contributing to the prolongation of the hostilities”.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the call was “constructive and substantive” adding that “Putin’s position is well known. It’s consistent, and he has spoken about the need to address the root causes.”

But Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said the Nordic leaders’ call with Putin offered “nothing new” to end the Ukraine conflict, saying that European countries were simply seeking a role in negotiations.

Meanwhile, responding to proposals for direct talks between Putin and Zelenskyy, Russian presidential aide Yury Ushakov said: “The current leader in Kyiv is not legitimate.”

“If Zelenskyy truly wants to hold direct talks, he should come to Moscow, where all necessary conditions will be provided for him, including security,” Ushakov added.

The Norwegian and Finnish leaders’ call with Putin was greeted with scepticism by some European leaders.

“My impression is that everyone wants peace, except for Putin himself. I have quite low expectations for this type of conversation,” Sweden’s Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson told local media.

He said some European leaders had not been informed.

Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen warned against individual diplomatic approaches to Moscow, saying European countries must maintain a united position. “I think Europe should stick together rather than going solo,” she said.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said he told Stubb and Stoere that “absolute caution and vigilance are necessary in such contacts”.

In a post on X, Lithuania’s Foreign Affairs Minister Kestutis Budrys said Europe must be at the table when peace in Ukraine is negotiated, “but not as a collection of fragmented voices”.

“Any contact with Russia must be backed by a united position, real leverage and a list of European demands,” Budrys said.

articles.title: ‘Russia is already part of who I am’: African students in Moscow
articles.summary: As the Russia-Africa Summit gets under way, students in the capital say education is helping to build ties.
articles.body:
Moscow, Russia – Moscow’s Patrice Lumumba Peoples’ Friendship University – better known as RUDN – offers a view of a relationship often discussed in the language of diplomacy, trade and security.

On the eve of the Russia-Africa Summit, due to begin on Wednesday in the capital Moscow, RUDN’s corridors are crowded with students speaking Russian, English, Arabic and dozens of African languages.

There are national celebrations, cultural showcases, food from across the continent and student clubs that turn the campus into what one graduate calls a “mini-city”.

For Africans who have come to study, work and build careers in Russia, the relationship is not an abstract geopolitical project. It is shaped by friendships, education, professional ambitions and the daily experience of life in Moscow.

Keturah Musonda, a Zambian medical graduate, said she has not regretted coming to Russia.

“I think Moscow is one of the best cities in the world,” she said, praising its transport system, the range of events and the opportunities she found beyond the classroom. Her student years at RUDN were filled with theatre, singing, student unions and medical studies. “My student life was quite colourful,” she said.

But it is Russia’s healthcare system that has left the strongest impression on her. Keturah points to the accessibility of ambulances, the investment in specialised equipment and testing, and the particular attention paid to paediatrics.

“In my country, I have never called an ambulance. No one in my family has ever called an ambulance,” she said.

In Moscow, she was struck by specialised children’s clinics and by a system in which paediatric care is treated as a priority. She hopes African countries can invest more heavily in specialist medicine, rather than relying on overstretched general departments inside large hospitals.

Her own journey was made possible through a Russian government scholarship programme, which allows foreign applicants to apply online, submit documents through Russian cultural centres and national authorities, and compete for university places in Russia.

For Moscow, such programmes are an investment in long-term links. For students like Keturah, they are a route to qualifications and experience they hope to take home.

Chinyama Kazombo, another Zambian medical student, describes Russia as a place where he can realise his potential. Over five years, he has made friends from China, Asia, Russia and across Africa, while participating in student events that introduce Russians to Zambian culture.

Zambia’s independence anniversary, he said, was celebrated in Moscow with dance, exhibitions and national traditions.

The ultimate goal is not simply a Russian diploma.

Zambia needs qualified doctors and other specialists, he said, and the education he receives in Russia could help him serve people back home.

Yet Russia will remain part of his life: “I’ll be working with Russians through my entire life … Russia is already part of who I am.”

For Abobakr Mohamed Abbakar Khussein from Sudan, a lecturer at a Moscow university, relations between Russia and Africa are moving in a pragmatic direction, even if they have not yet reached their full potential.

He sees African governments seeking economic links, security cooperation, energy and agricultural partnerships with countries that respect their sovereignty.

Sudan’s relationship with Russia, he noted, dates back 70 years, beginning shortly after Sudanese independence. He pointed to Russian archaeological work around Sudan’s ancient pyramids, as well as the training of Sudanese specialists in medicine, agriculture, the humanities and linguistics. He also sees potential in mining and nuclear cooperation, including with Rosatom.

But he also highlighted the vulnerability created by the war in Ukraine.

Disruption to Russian and Ukrainian grain and cooking-oil exports threatens food security across Africa, he said. His conclusion is direct: African countries need peace, dependable trade routes and practical partnerships.

Aaron Kasonde, a lecturer and assistant professor at RUDN from Zambia, believes agriculture could become one of the most important areas of Russia-Africa cooperation. Africa has vast arable land and a fast-growing, youthful population – the average age is about 19, he said.

The continent needs fertilisers, irrigation systems, investment and technology, Kasonde added.

Several African states remain net food importers, despite having the land and labour needed to produce more. Russia, one of the world’s major wheat and fertiliser producers, could contribute not only through grain exports but through technologies that help African farmers raise yields and build lasting food security, Kasonde believes.

For Hafi Ahmed from Kenya, the next frontier is broader economic cooperation.

Kenya may be smaller than Russia in territory and population, she said, but it has an educated workforce, skilled doctors and nurses, natural resources and significant growth potential. Cultural exchange also matters. She believes Kenyans and Russians have more in common than many assume – an impression reinforced by her close friendship with a Russian.

What unites these voices is neither blind enthusiasm nor a demand that Africa choose geopolitical sides. They want cooperation to produce measurable benefits: Qualified professionals, modern healthcare, food security, technology, jobs and cultural diversity.

Whether the partner is Russia, China, the United States or Europe, the question for African countries is whether that relationship supports national interests and development. On a campus built around international friendship, that is also the message shaping the future of Russia-Africa ties.

articles.title: Spain train crash: Govt blames 'human error' by operator — what led to collision?
articles.summary: The Spanish government has blamed a \"possible human error\" by a railway operator as the cause of a deadly collision between two high-speed trains in the
articles.body: The Spanish government has blamed a "possible human error" by a railway operator as the cause of a deadly collision between two high-speed trains in the central province of Toledo.The preliminary assessment points to a failure in the main signalling system, which may have contributed to the crash in which over 64 people were killed.The collision involved an AVE train and an Iryo train on the Madrid-Seville route, disrupting rail services connecting Madrid with Ciudad Real and Andalusia."A human error by an Adif operator in the face of a breakdown of the main signaling system is the possible cause of the accident," sources from the government led by Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez told Okdiario.Spain's transport minister said that the train's control system failed after an issue in the computer communication, prompting an immediate halt to train services.According to initial analyses by the government sources, the automated safety system could fail while switching to manual mode, which is why the trains came to a stop and service resumed under human control. And that is where the error occurred.A passenger traveling in one of the rear cars of one of the trains told EL PAÍS that he felt a “strong impact” about 40 minutes into the trip. The collision occurred at kilometer marker 118, between the towns of Mora, Orgaz, and Urda (Toledo).A decision to resume train operations was taken at 8.36, the transport minister added.Even experts suspect that a failure in the LZB Level 2 automatic signalling system may have forced operators to switch to manual control.Introduced in the 1980s when Spain's Madrid-Seville high-speed line was built, LZB is a train safety and control system that is now largely outdated.The line is undergoing a technological upgrade, including the installation of the newer ERTMS Level 2 system and modernisation of its signalling and telecommunications infrastructure. Rail operator ADIF has said the work is nearing completion.Apart from the minister's remark, the officials have not yet explained exactly how the signalling breakdown occurred or what action may have led to the crash. Thefore, the possibility of human error remains a preliminary explanation.Padilla has also said it is unclear why one of the trains appeared to be stopped on the track. Investigators will have to establish the sequence of events, including whether the signalling failure and the operator's actions directly contributed to the collision.What happened on the railway lineThe crash took place on Wednesday morning near Urda, in Toledo province. Regional government spokesperson Esther Padilla confirmed that an AVE train collided with an Iryo train on the Madrid-Seville line.According to Spanish state broadcaster TVE, one of the trains appeared to be stationary when the collision occurred. The impact sent several carriages down an embankment, prompting emergency services to rush to the scene.Padilla said officials were still trying to establish why one train appeared to have stopped and how the collision unfolded. The Iryo train was carrying 146 passengers and a baby, while the AVE train had 397 people on board.Spain's rail infrastructure operator ADIF suspended services on the affected routes as rescue and emergency response operations continued.Expressing shock over what he called a "serious train accident", Spanish PM Pedro Sánchez said: "Emergency services are working on the ground to assist those affected and ensure their safety, in coordination with all the involved administrations. My affection, solidarity, and support to all the victims and their families."Second major rail tragedy in monthsThe crash has renewed concerns about rail safety in Spain, which has one of Europe's most extensive high-speed railway networks.In January, another deadly train disaster in southern Spain killed 45 people after a train derailed and collided with an oncoming train. articles.title: Workers should be able to know colleagues' salaries, rights body says
articles.summary: Employees should legally be able to find out what their co-workers are earning, the UK's equality watchdog says
articles.body:
Employees should legally be able to find out what their colleagues are earning, the UK's equality watchdog has said.

Bosses should be required to respond to questionaires about colleagues' pay to cut pay discrimination, the Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) has proposed .

In addition, employers should be prevented from asking about current salary when offering a job to stop a history of discrimination from carrying on, it said.

Employers in the UK are currently allowed to ask you how much you get paid in your current role, but applicants are under no obligation to tell them .

At present, employers do not have to respond to employee requests for salary information about colleagues.

The EHRC urged lawmakers to make it compulsory for employers to provide information including colleagues' basic pay and hours worked, how employees' pay compares with each other, and information about bonuses, overtime, shift-premiums and performance-related pay, within a specific timeframe.

The rights watchdog argued that this would help cut pay discrimination, especially against women.

Women would also benefit from employers publishing salary details in job adverts, the EHRC has said previously .

The job interview question you don't have to answer

John Kirkpatrick, the EHRC chief executive, told the BBC that employers should not be able to ask about salary history when setting pay.

"When they do, what tends to happen is that can embed a history of disadvantage or discrimination in future salaries," he said.

While employers should be able to offer a competitive salary, this should not "create a pattern that discriminates," he said.

The Fawcett Society, which campaigns for women and gender equality, has previously said that asking the question risked maintaining historic unfair differences in pay due to gender, race and disability inequality.

Rather than offering a salary based on skills, experience and performance, it meant employers rewarded an individual's perceived worth and negotiating skills instead, the society said.

articles.title: China takes Mbappé’s apology ‘seriously’ after backlash over his ‘Chinese dictator’ comments
articles.summary: China’s Foreign Ministry said Wednesday it has taken soccer star Kylian Mbappé’s apology “seriously” for comments considered to be disrespectful of Mao Zedong, the founding leader of Communist China, as the fallout over the issue continues.
articles.body: China’s Foreign Ministry said Wednesday it has taken soccer star Kylian Mbappé’s apology “seriously” for comments considered to be disrespectful of Mao Zedong, the founding leader of Communist China, as the fallout over the issue continues. Mbappé faced a backlash Tuesday over comments he made in an online interview, losing brand deals with at least three different Chinese companies. Beverage maker Dongpeng, dairy giant Mengniu and cheese maker Milkground said in similarly worded statements that they were ending agreements with the star forward, each saying they oppose “any words and actions that hurt national sentiment.” “We take seriously the apology he has made,” said Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Guo Jiakun in a daily press briefing Wednesday. It remains to be seen whether Mbappé’s apology will help him regain the brand deals or other businesses he lost Tuesday. His team’s games remained unavailable to viewers in China Wednesday. “Of course, once a public figure’s speech and actions cross the limit, or step on a red line, … he becomes a brand’s negative asset,” said the Communist Party’s official mouthpiece, the People’s Daily, in an online column Wednesday. “It is owing to principles and the necessity of business logic that Chinese platforms and companies take firm actions to cut off such a relationship.” The incident is the latest in a string of cases in which China has leveraged its economic clout to compel foreign companies and individuals to apologize for perceived slights. In 2019, Chinese state television ceased broadcasting NBA games after then-Houston Rockets general manager Daryl Morey tweeted support for anti-government protesters in Hong Kong. China Media Group also said that it has suspended broadcasts of matches in the Spanish league and other games featuring the French player and demanded an apology from La Liga, Mbappé and his club, Real Madrid. Mbappé issued an apology Tuesday, saying, “My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world.” “I apologize to everyone my words have upset,” Mbappé said in a statement. “This was absolutely not my intention. I have deep respect for the Chinese people and their history, and I am sincerely sorry.” On Tuesday, Spanish league president Javier Tebas quickly issued a public apology and stressed La Liga’s commitment to preserving its partnerships with China. Real Madrid apologized later on Wednesday, joining Mbappé in expressing regret over the player’s remarks and reiterating its respect for the Chinese people. CMG said it received the apology from Real Madrid, without adding further comment. Earlier, it demanded a formal apology, saying the club’s stance that a player was entitled to his personal opinion was unacceptable. In a video clip, Mbappé is asked about his favorite meme of himself, and the soccer star replies that it was “a video someone made of a guy … I think he was a Chinese dictator” before the video shows an altered image depicting Mbappé’s face on the blue-suited body of Mao Zedong. Soccer fans online jokingly call the star — who’s said to overshadow many of his teammates and even the teams he plays on — a dictator, and memes showing him as Mao or other autocratic leaders are widely circulated. Mao Zedong was a revolutionary who led the Communist Party during its crucial early days, winning a civil war against the ruling Nationalist Party in China, and then founding the modern-day People’s Republic of China. Mao is revered by many, even today. However, he left behind a complex legacy of authoritarian rule, having led campaigns, like the 1959-63 Great Leap Forward and the 1966-76 Cultural Revolution, which killed an estimated 31 million people through starvation and persecution. But China’s online censorship apparatus meant that even though news about Mbappé’s lost brand deals was trending Tuesday, not everyone knew what he said. Comments about top leaders are considered sensitive and his comment was not translated by the brands or state media who criticized his remarks. “Maybe he said something he shouldn’t have again and hurt people’s feelings here in China,” said He Xiaodou on Wednesday. The Beijing finance worker said he heard about the controversy, but did not know what it was about exactly. “I just vaguely got the impression that it might have been something political.” Others who did know took the comments in stride. “I think maybe some people or some companies are overreacting on this issue,” said Li Zhi, a Beijing lawyer. “It’s not a big deal. It’s not the first time this happened.”

articles.title: 63 in 100 Indian pilots may be sleepy during dawn landings after 10-hour night shift, safety review warns
articles.summary: MUMBAI: About 63 in 100 Indian pilots were predicted to be sleepy when they land at dawn after the legally permitted maximum night duty of 10 hours,
articles.body: MUMBAI: About 63 in 100 Indian pilots were predicted to be sleepy when they land at dawn after the legally permitted maximum night duty of 10 hours, according to a review by Safety Matters Foundation, a not-for-profit aviation safety group.The question it attempted to answer was: How many pilots are sleepy as they begin the last landing? For Europe, which has day flights, that number was 16 in 100.The study’s objective was to examine whether India’s rules on pilot working hours keep pilots awake enough to fly safely.“Short answer, by day, mostly yes. At night and late in the evening, often not,” it said, adding that a duty can follow every roster rule and yet leave most of the crew sleepy.The message was that a legal duty period can still be a tiring duty. The fix is in the rules, not in the pilots, it said.“The review does not say flying in India is unsafe, or that any pilot was unsafe.” The 63-in-100 figure is a forecast for a type of duty, here 9pm to 7am, not a count of named pilots, it clarified. It comes from a sleep and body-clock model run on legal limits and the anonymised rosters of 13 pilots.Its author and founder, Capt Amit Singh FRAeS, said the findings match what pilots have long reported. “Indian pilots have told us, survey after survey, that they are too tired to fly,” Capt Singh said.“The science explains why. India's rules leave the late evening open, allow a 13-hour day without asking when it starts, and file most fatigue reports away as 'perceived'. The rules count the hours. The body counts the clock.”The foundation's surveys of Indian pilots, with 542 respondents in 2022 and 530 in 2024, point in the same direction. Seventy-one in 100 said they had often been too tired for cockpit duty, and 66 in 100 reported unplanned sleep or microsleeps on duty.The review tested India against ICAO's requirement that duty rules be based on science, knowledge and operational experience. It rated India as “partly met” on science and knowledge, and “not shown” on its own experience.India handles deep-night duties well, said the release issued by the foundation. Duties touching midnight to 6am are limited to 10 hours and two landings. By day, however, the picture changes.“India allows 13 hours as a routine day, for any start up to 10:30am, with no extra safeguard.” A day ending just before midnight may include six landings, and on a legal day with a landing at 11:30pm, 55 to 77 in 100 pilots are predicted to be sleepy.“Two forces drive tiredness. From the moment you wake, sleep pressure builds like a phone battery draining, only sleep recharges it. Separately, the body clock raises and lowers alertness like a tide, lowest between about 2 and 6am. Night flying combines a flat battery with a low tide. And when sleep is cut short night after night, the shortfall carries over, like a debt,” the study said.It drew a comparison with alcohol. “India takes a pilot off the roster for any detectable alcohol and suspends the licence above 0.009%.”After 17 to 19 hours awake, a person performs about as badly as at 0.05% blood alcohol, more than five times that level, it added.The review also questioned how the rules were made. The DGCA's 2023 study, which formed the basis for the 2024 rules, “reviewed rosters and reports only”, with no wrist-worn sleep monitors and no measurement of alertness, the release said.Five weeks after the night rules took full effect in late 2025, the DGCA suspended them for one large operator. The government told Parliament that operators' safety risk assessments had been checked, but none had been published, the foundation said.Investigators have raised similar concerns. In the 2010 Mangalore crash that killed 158 people, the Court of Inquiry found that the captain had slept for most of the recorded cruise. In 2013, investigators found that fatigue contributed to an error in a serious incident in Mumbai.The foundation urged three changes: duty limits set by start time; penalty-free fatigue reporting, along with an independent study of pilot sleep and alertness; and publication of the evidence behind every exemption, with an end date.“The review does not say flying in India is unsafe, or that any pilot was unsafe.” The 63-in-100 figure is a forecast for a type of duty, here 9pm to 7am, not a count of named pilots, it clarified.It comes from a sleep and body-clock model run on legal limits and the anonymised rosters of 13 pilots.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Mumbai | Silver Rate in Mumbai | Bank Holidays in Mumbai | Public Holidays in Mumbai | Mumbai AQI | Weather in Mumbai | Petrol Price in Mumbai | Diesel Price in Mumbai | CNG Price in Mumbai | LPG Price in MumbaiStay updated with the latest Mumbai news. articles.title: Pip payment denied for terminally ill mum with cancer
articles.summary: Rachael Field, from Rhondda Cynon Taf, had her tongue and voicebox removed and windpipe reconstructed.
articles.body:
A terminally ill mum who has been given three years to live has been denied disability benefit despite being unable to eat, talk, dress or use the toilet independently.

Rachael Field, 56, from Rhondda Cynon Taf, who has tongue cancer, was first diagnosed six years ago.

She uses a feeding tube, has had her tongue and voice box removed, and had her windpipe reconstructed using chest tissue. Field also has mobility issues.

Earlier this year, she was denied Personal Independence Payment (Pip), to support people with disability-related extra costs.

The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) said it needed further evidence to complete the claim and was sorry for "any distress" to the family.

Field said she has had cancer four times in six years, and now cannot do anything for herself.

"I need help to wash, dress and use the bathroom. I can only walk a few steps with help. I cannot eat or drink, everything has to go through my feeding tube," she added.

The former factory worker was forced to stop working following her terminal diagnosis, and her family has been managing the financial strain.

Field applied for Pip in May, but it was denied as she was awarded zero points across all assessed categories.

Pip is a benefit people with long-term illnesses and disabilities can claim if they need help with extra costs associated with living, work and care. Eligibility is determined through an assessment.

Under the current system, claimants are scored on a zero to 12 scale by a health professional on everyday tasks such as washing, getting dressed and preparing food.

Field's family said repeated rescheduling of the assessment process caused delays, and that despite lodging an appeal several months ago, they are still awaiting an outcome.

Field said the treatment she received from her medical test "has been outstanding" but has an issue with "the system Pip uses to assess people".

She said: "People need the help while they are alive."

Her daughter, Kyra Hawkins-Field, 20, said it is "ridiculous" that her mum has not been able to claim Pip and does not want her "stressing about money" while she only has "a couple of years left".

She criticised the benefits assessment process and said it was too reliant on a checklist, and did not reflect people's real-life struggles.

"They've basically turned around and said, 'we think you're fine'," she said.

Hawkins-Field said her dad Eddie has become the family's "superhero", working full-time and then visiting his wife in hospital every day.

The couple married 15 years ago after meeting when they both worked in a factory. They enjoy visiting towns across Wales, and still hope to visit Scotland and Ireland one day.

Hawkins-Field said her mum likes the "little things in life", but "loves doing jigsaw puzzles, big, really, really difficult, intricate jigsaw puzzles" and reading.

Hawkins-Field launched a GoFundMe appeal with the aim of raising £1,000 to help her mum enjoy what time she has left with her family, including some trips around the UK, while she still can.

A DWP spokesperson said: "We're sorry for any distress Ms Field and her family are feeling at this difficult time.

"We have been unable to complete the claim as we need further evidence from Ms Field. We have attempted to contact her in order to resolve the situation and will continue to do so."

Field's family said they were in discussion with the DWP.

articles.title: Attacker shouting 'Allahu Akbar' killed outside Israeli Embassy in Serbia, police say
articles.summary: An assailant shouting Allahu Akbar attacked a Gendarmerie officer outside the Israeli Embassy in Belgrade before being fatally shot by the officer.
articles.body: An assailant armed with two knives attacked a member of Serbia's Gendarmerie guarding the Israeli Embassy in Belgrade shortly after midnight Wednesday, prompting the officer to fatally shoot the attacker in self-defense, according to Serbian authorities. The assailant, who was a minor, allegedly shouted "Allahu Akbar" — or "God is great" in Arabic — as he slashed the officer in the face, leaving the officer "slightly injured." Interior Minister Ivica Dacic said authorities are treating the incident as a terrorist attack, adding that security forces had been monitoring the assailant. Dacic said the attacker supported ISIS and displayed a black flag bearing the terrorist group's symbol on his Instagram account. The attacker was believed to be Serbian and from the town of Sabac, Dacic added. HALIMA SALMAN CONVICTED OF RECEIVING ISIS MILITARY TRAINING IN SYRIA, FACES 10 YEARS IN PRISON Israel's foreign ministry confirmed the "attempted terrorist attack," and said the incident was under investigation by the relevant authorities. "The attacker was neutralized by local police. No embassy personnel were injured, and the mission was closed at the time of the incident, which occurred late at night," the statement said. articles.title: King Charles faces calls for slavery reparations as he arrives in Bahamas on official Caribbean trip
articles.summary: King Charles III arrived in the Bahamas as part of a nine-day trip to the Caribbean, where he faces calls for an apology and slavery reparations.
articles.body: King Charles III arrived in the Bahamas on Tuesday as part of a nine-day trip to the Caribbean, where he faces calls for an apology and slavery reparations. It’s his first official visit to the Bahamas as king, with the archipelago’s government closing all public schools on the island of New Providence to welcome him. The Bahamian police and armed forces strode out to greet Charles in lockstep, some wearing pith helmets. Charles stepped out in a light gray suit and donned sunglasses as he greeted Governor-General Dame Cynthia A. Pratt and Prime Minister Philip Davis. The monarch then traveled to Clifford Park, which he last officially visited as Prince of Wales in 1973 to grant the Bahamas independence after 300 years of British rule. Members of the Bahamas’ Rastafarian community and others lined a road near Clifford Park in protest, demanding reparations. “Pay us what you owe us!” one woman cried out. “I stand in memory of the horrors and the atrocities committed against Black people.” Meanwhile, a cheering crowd awaited Charles as he arrived at the park, with dozens of young students waving small Bahamian flags ahead of a cultural event that included children singing and playing music. “We know that some of what is best in Bahamian culture today, the most joyful, the most hopeful, the most bright, was born out of darkness,” Charles said in his first public remarks since arriving in the Bahamas. “It is only right that we should acknowledge the great suffering and injustices of the past in these islands and beyond, even as we rejoice in the successes of the present.” Jamaica recently took its case for reparations to Charles, and the case has since been referred to the United Kingdom’s highest court of appeal for the Caribbean island. The British government, however, has consistently rejected demands for either an apology or reparations. While in the Bahamas, Charles also is expected to visit a nature site and meet with the Royal Bahamas Defense Force as well as government officials and civil society leaders. Some in the Bahamas hope his visit will draw attention to an ongoing environmental struggle on an island that forms part of the Exuma cays. Eric Carey, former executive director of the Bahamas National Trust, said the Save Exuma Alliance is fighting a development on Sampson Cay that he called “ill-advised” and “out of scale.” He noted that the development calls for a “massive” sea wall and the dredging of sea grass and coral reefs. “This is not a position of antidevelopment; our country is a tourism-based economy,” Carey said in a phone interview. “Our point is that there are larger islands where larger scale developments could be more effectively and efficiently constructed.” The case is currently in the hands of the Bahamas Supreme Court, but Carey said he hopes Charles will raise awareness about the issue. “King Charles has a long history of defending the environment, talking about climate change,” Carey said. “He’s visiting … one of the most vulnerable regions in the world.” During his speech at Clifford Park, Charles acknowledged the climate challenges that the Bahamas and other nations face. “We cannot escape the fact that the journey ahead contains some treacherous shoals, in particular in an island nation where 90% of the land sits below two meters,” Charles said. “There is perhaps nowhere better than the Bahamas to understand the reality of climate change.” Charles is scheduled to spend three days in the Bahamas and then fly to the South American country of Guyana on Oct. 29, where he will spend two days in the former British colony whose president has said he wants an apology. He is then scheduled to fly to Antigua and Barbuda on Oct. 30 for the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting, where Queen Camilla will join him. Talks are expected to focus on climate, trade and development, but some Caribbean leaders have said slavery reparations should dominate conversations.

articles.title: Israel’s election: The battle between change and anti-Palestinian sentiment
articles.summary: With both blocs short of a majority, parties face a choice: to break the taboo on Arab allies or return to the polls.
articles.body:
With Israel’s governing and opposition blocs failing to secure a majority in Israel’s election , and neither appearing ready to ally with Arab parties that could allow them to form a coalition, speculation is growing over the future shape of the government.

The vote on Tuesday, billed as one of the most important in Israel’s history, saw turnout reach 77.7 percent of eligible voters – the highest level since 1999.

With nearly 80 percent of votes counted by Wednesday afternoon, the outgoing coalition led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, centred around his Likud party, had secured 54 seats, short of the 61 needed to establish a governing coalition.

Former military chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot’s self-styled Zionist opposition, drawing from parties as diverse as Yair Golan’s relatively left-wing Democrats and Avigdor Lieberman’s hard-right Yisrael Beiteinu, had 49 seats, also short of a governing majority in the 120-strong Knesset.

Holding the balance of power , in theory at least, are the Arab-dominated Ra’am and Joint List, with 17 seats, more than enough to give either bloc a majority with which to appoint a speaker, pass legislation and form a working government.

Those figures are not final, however, with the final tally expected by Friday and official results formally published on November 4 .

What happens next is a matter of procedure as much as politics.

President Isaac Herzog will consult party leaders on who they want as prime minister, before tasking the candidate he believes has the best chance of forming a government. That candidate has 28 days to build a coalition, with a possible 14-day extension. If they fail, the mandate can pass to another member of parliament, and if that also fails, the Knesset is dissolved and Israelis return to the polls, with the current cabinet staying on as caretaker.

Turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel, who account for one-fifth of the total population, reached about 80 percent, according to some estimates, also above the 1999 figures.

Analysts said the surge was propelled by the harsh treatment of the Israeli-Palestinian minority by the Likud-led government, which increased significantly following the Hamas-led attack of October 7, 2023 that triggered Israel’s genocidal war against Palestinians in Gaza. Netanyahu’s outgoing government is the most right-wing in Israeli history, featuring far-right figures such as National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, whose policies and rhetoric against Palestinians have essentially made him a recruiting sergeant for the pro-Arab parties.

Analysts also attributed the strong performance to a well-organised campaign that targeted the demands of Israel’s Palestinian community and the opportunity for a greater voice in the Knesset.

“Having just two well-organised lists significantly improved their vote-collecting efficiency and ground-level mobilisation – particularly for Ra’am, the Islamist party, which ran a much more efficient campaign than usual,” Roi Zur, a lecturer at Essex University and specialist in Israeli voting behaviour and election strategies, told Al Jazeera.

“The broader shift, however, comes down to how voters view their place in Israeli politics,” he added, “especially following October 7 and the subsequent war,” Zur added.

“On one hand, many voters feel more integrated into Israeli society, driven by shifts in how the public processed both the October 7 attacks and the government’s subsequent policies, making them feel more invested in the political system.”

However, both blocs ran campaigns that critics have described as profoundly racist. Likud spent much of the election race making unsubstantiated claims that the opposition was planning to form a government reliant on Arab parties after the vote, while petitioning to bar the Joint List from running.

On the opposition side, Lieberman ruled out a coalition with either Arab or ultra-Orthodox (Haredi) parties, while Together’s Naftali Bennett, whose 2021-22 coalition included Ra’am, told an activists’ conference there was “no mandate” to form a government with Arab parties after the October 7 attack.

“The ‘opposition’ bloc continues to think you beat Bibi by being Bibi-lite, offering no substantive alternative or hope,” said former government adviser Daniel Levy, using a common nickname for the Israeli prime minister. “Really, the opposition got what they deserved,” he added, arguing it would have won the election if its members’ commitment to removing Netanyahu had outweighed their “commitment to a racist ethno-centric version of Zionism”.

Levy sees four possible scenarios ahead for either bloc, listed in no particular order: the possibility of a new election; Likud drawing enough defectors from the right of the opposition to form a government; a so-called “unity government” led by Netanyahu that draws on the right across the Knesset; and “Eisenkot and company biting the bullet and using the anti-Netanyahu majority to form a minority government with Arab support,” he said.

“Even if they announce it’s time-limited before another election, the Arab parties’ asking price will not be particularly high,” he said, with the caveat that he considered such a coalition unlikely.

The chance of defection amidst what is seen as a highly polarised society remains unclear.

Much of the Eisenkot bloc’s campaign, and by extension its vote, rested upon opposition to the de facto exemption from military service offered by the Likud-led government to the Haredi parties in return for their support in the Knesset. Rivalling the pressure to extend the draft to Israel’s ultra-Orthodox youth were the calls for an independent inquiry into the government’s alleged security failings before the October 7 attack, calls rendered more pressing in light of the reports of the alleged advance warnings given by the United Arab Emirates and Egypt.

“I think it would be very hard to see Eisenkot working with anyone in Netanyahu’s camp because of the ultra-Orthodox draft issue and because of October 7,” said Mairav Zonszein, an analyst with the Crisis Group. “His main demands are a state commission of inquiry and a universal draft for everyone, so he couldn’t work with a lot of the partners there, including Netanyahu,” she added.

“However, Bennett and Lieberman are different stories. Bennett has swerved once before,” she said, referring to him reneging on election promises and working with Ra’am in 2021.

“Lieberman, as much as he hates Netanyahu, is also a very hard-right politician,” she said of the likelihood of Yisrael Beiteinu allying with Likud to prevent any liberal-leaning politics.

For now, though, speculation continues. For some, including Levy, that includes the possibility of the Netanyahu government seeking a military escalation, potentially against Iran, as a pretext to establish an emergency government.

For others, such as Israeli political psychologist Daniel Bar Tal of Tel Aviv University, the future rests upon the more prosaic mathematics of a government coalition.

“It is a very challenging moment in the history of Israel,” he said, reflecting on the many opportunities to gain power missed by the opposition.

“It is hard to know [what will happen] because the majority of Israelis are rightists, racists, religious and nationalists,” he said, before cutting to the heart of the dilemma faced by many in Israel on the day after the election: “They want change but do not want to cooperate with Arab parties.”

articles.title: An 127-room Long Island castle featured in Taylor Swift’s “Blank Space” video sold for $72 million at auction, nearly half its $137 million appraisal, after bankruptcy proceedings put the historic estate’s future in doubt
articles.summary: A century of lavish parties, celebrity weddings and cinematic appearances has not been enough to shield one of America’s most storied estates from
articles.body: A century of lavish parties, celebrity weddings and cinematic appearances has not been enough to shield one of America’s most storied estates from financial turmoil. Oheka Castle, the grand Long Island mansion that once embodied the extravagance of the Gilded Age, has entered a new chapter after changing hands at auction for $72 million, significantly below its estimated value of $137 million. The sale brings an end to the ownership era of developer Gary Melius, who spent decades restoring and maintaining the historic property. For its new owners, however, the acquisition presents an unusual opportunity: preserving a landmark while potentially unlocking a lucrative residential development.A castle sold under financial pressureLocated in Huntington, New York, Oheka Castle sold to Ronald Browning and Paul Alflen, partners at Gold Coast Property & Estate Management, following an auction organised by Concierge Auctions in collaboration with the Modlin Group.According to Realtor, the property attracted seven participants, including developers, hospitality operators and wealthy buyers interested in acquiring a rare historic estate. Its 2025 appraisal, prepared during Chapter 11 bankruptcy proceedings, placed its value at $137 million, making the $72 million winning bid a substantial discount.The financial difficulties behind the sale were considerable. As reported by the New York Post, Oheka's hotel, restaurant and event operations were left with less than $60 in their bank account, no cash on hand and more than $63.5 million in debt. The mounting liabilities ultimately forced the property into a court-supervised sale.The development opportunity behind the dealBeyond the castle's historic appeal, its development potential adds another dimension to the purchase. Huntington authorities have approved plans for 95 luxury condominiums on the easternmost five acres of the larger 23-acre property.The 2025 appraisal included development rights, so the new owners could build residential and continue the estate's hospitality business, the Realtor said. The project could be a major commercial opportunity at unit prices over $1.8 million.Before the auction, investment firm Taconic Capital was considered a strong contender because it held the property's defaulted mortgage. The firm had a court-authorised credit bid of approximately $61 million, allowing it to use the outstanding loan balance towards a potential purchase rather than compete entirely with fresh cash.The New York Post also reported that Taconic owned an adjacent 13.3-acre development site, raising the possibility of combining the properties for a larger residential project. The final sale to Browning and Alflen leaves the future of these development opportunities in the hands of the new owners.From gilded age excess to Hollywood fameOheka Castle was built by financier Otto Kahn in the early 20th century, when America's wealthiest industrialists competed to construct increasingly extravagant estates along Long Island's Gold Coast.Kahn, who faced exclusion from local country clubs because he was Jewish, created a private enclave with extensive grounds and recreational facilities. The mansion became synonymous with lavish entertaining, hosting prominent figures from entertainment, music and high society.Its history extended well beyond the Jazz Age. During the Second World War, the property served as a school for radio operators before later being used as a retreat for New York City sanitation workers. It subsequently found another life as a film location, including as the setting for Xanadu in Orson Welles' Citizen Kane.Taylor Swift and a lasting celebrity connectionOheka's cultural relevance has continued into the modern era. Taylor Swift filmed her Blank Space music video at the estate, using its imposing architecture and formal gardens to create the opulent setting that helped define the production's visual identity.According to Realtor, the castle has remained a destination for celebrity celebrations and high-profile events. Its guest suites, grand ballroom and landscaped grounds have also made it a sought-after setting for weddings, photography shoots and private gatherings.Among its notable wedding celebrations was Kevin Jonas' 2009 marriage, which took place amid a major snowstorm. Former politician Anthony Weiner also married Huma Abedin at the estate in a ceremony officiated by former US president Bill Clinton. Despite its change in ownership, existing wedding and event bookings must be honoured until at least March 2028, as reported by Realtor.What comes next for Oheka?The auction marks a turning point for an estate that has survived changing fortunes, shifting uses and decades of expensive upkeep. Its new owners inherit not only a landmark with an extraordinary past but also a hospitality operation and development rights that could shape its future.Images Courtesy: Instagram/taylorswift/ohekacastleReady to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: A California foster-care survivor says he reported abuse as a child in 2006 but officials failed to act; nearly 20 years later, an appeals court reversed the dismissal of his negligence lawsuit against Alameda County
articles.summary: A California man who alleges that he was sexually abused while in foster care and that officials failed to protect him has won a significant legal victory
articles.body: A California man who alleges that he was sexually abused while in foster care and that officials failed to protect him has won a significant legal victory after an appeals court revived his negligence lawsuit against Alameda County. The California Court of Appeal, First Appellate District, Division Four, reversed the dismissal on October 26, 2026. According to the court’s published opinion, available on Justia, the man, identified as K.S., alleged that he reported the abuse to a group home supervisor in 2006, when he was 12 years old, but no investigation or protective action followed. The ruling allows his lawsuit to proceed.Foster child alleged abuse continued after he reported itK.S. was in Alameda County’s foster care system when the county placed him in a group home in 2006. According to his complaint, he was sexually abused by an adult male staff member between 2006 and 2007, when he was approximately 12 to 13 years old. K.S. alleged that he reported the abuse to a supervisor at the facility, who was an agent of the county. However, he claimed that officials failed to investigate his allegations or take measures to protect him from further harm. His complaint further alleged that, instead of safeguarding him, staff members penalised him by revoking privileges, administering or increasing medication, and placing him in a quiet room where the alleged perpetrator could continue to access him.These details formed part of K.S.’s allegations, which the appeals court had to accept as true for the limited purpose of reviewing the dismissal at the pleading stage. The ruling did not establish that the allegations had been proven.Lawsuit accused county of broader failures in supervisionK.S. filed his negligence lawsuit in 2022, seeking to hold Alameda County responsible for the alleged failures of its employees and agents. His complaint argued that the county had not adequately protected children in its care from foreseeable sexual abuse. Beyond the response to his individual report, K.S. alleged wider shortcomings in the foster care system. These included inadequate supervision of group homes and contracted agencies, insufficient training and oversight of caseworkers, and failures to establish and enforce appropriate child-safety standards.He also alleged that officials failed to conduct adequate visits and checks, assess the safety of placements, and implement policies designed to prevent sexual abuse. The lawsuit sought to hold the county vicariously liable for negligence by employees or agents whose conduct allegedly contributed to his injuries. Alameda County challenged the lawsuit, arguing that governmental immunity protected it from liability for the conduct described in the complaint. The trial court accepted that argument and granted judgment on the pleadings, effectively dismissing the case before a full examination of the evidence.Appeals court examined governmental immunityThe dispute centred on Section 820.2 of the California Government Code, which provides immunity to public employees for injuries resulting from certain discretionary acts. Under the relevant provisions, a public entity may also be protected when its employees are immune. The county argued that decisions made by social workers about investigating abuse reports and determining what action to take involved discretion. It maintained that such decisions were protected by the statute.The appeals court acknowledged that decisions about whether to investigate allegations of child abuse and what protective measures to take can qualify for discretionary immunity. However, it explained that not every aspect of supervising a foster child necessarily involves a protected policy decision. The court distinguished between discretionary decisions, which involve a conscious assessment of competing risks and policy considerations, and ministerial or operational duties, such as certain routine monitoring and protective responsibilities.It found that K.S.’s complaint alleged a broader range of failures than simply an unsuccessful decision about how to investigate his report. These included alleged failures to recognise abuse, conduct appropriate background checks and take reasonable measures to protect a child from foreseeable harm. At the pleading stage, the court said it could not conclude that all the alleged acts and omissions necessarily resulted from a conscious exercise of discretion.Court sends negligence case back for further proceedingsThe appeals court also rejected the argument that the alleged punishment following K.S.’s report necessarily demonstrated that officials had carefully considered his allegations and deliberately decided against intervention. The judges explained that the complaint did not establish what considerations, if any, had informed the alleged response. Determining what happened would require a fuller examination of the facts, rather than assumptions made from the allegations alone.The court therefore reversed the trial court’s judgment. Its decision means K.S.’s negligence lawsuit can proceed to further proceedings, where the relevant facts and legal issues can be examined. The ruling does not establish the county’s liability or determine the ultimate outcome of the lawsuit. Instead, it addresses whether the case could be dismissed at such an early stage on the immunity grounds raised by the county.The decision highlights the legal distinction between protected government policy decisions and alleged failures in the day-to-day supervision and protection of children in foster care. For K.S., the reversal represents an opportunity to pursue his claims in court after alleging that his reports of abuse as a child did not result in the protection he needed.You use AI every day. articles.title: Eden Geothermal plans to drill four more wells in Cornwall
articles.summary: The Eden Project's partner organisation also proposes an increase in power generation capacity.
articles.body:
The UK's first geothermal power plant said it wants to increase the number of underground wells it was previously allowed from two to six.

Eden Geothermal, in Cornwall, said proposed changes to a previously approved planning application offered "a significant benefit in terms of increasing the renewable energy generated on site". Other changes were proposed to allow for an increase in generation capacity, it added.

Members of the public who live near the Eden Project have been invited to discuss the proposed changes at Trethurgy Village Hall on Wednesday between 15:00 GMT to 19:00 and 6 November from 15:00 to 18:00.

The planning application has a determination date of 18 November.

Eden Geothermal said key changes included increasing the size of an air-cooled condenser bank, reconfiguration of site buildings and the installation of two substations, rather than the one previously agreed with Cornwall Council, the Local Democracy Reporting Service reported.

The plant's water storage lagoon would be decreased in size if the changes were agreed.

Reaching about 5km (3.1miles/16,400 ft) below the Earth's surface, the current geothermal well taps into water temperatures of up to 200C (390F) to provide heating to Eden's greenhouses and rainforest biome.

The current well at Eden Geothermal has a vertical depth of just over 4.8km (3 miles).

A second similarly-sized well was also approved in December 2010, but has yet to be drilled.

Project bosses now want to drill four more wells in a bid to increase capacity "without the need to extend beyond the approved boundary or substantially alter what has already been approved".

A supporting report by Gilly Slater, on behalf of SLR Consulting Limited, stated: "The surface area of the site remains unchanged, such that the proposed amendments will not result in any impacts to the Tree Preservation Order area or the existing drainage system and strategy."

Cornwall Council's landscape team were supportive of Eden Geothermal's mitigation of likely effects of the proposals on the site itself and upon its wider landscape context.

They stated: "It should be noted that the development/construction phase of the project may involve disturbance through other environmental factors (dust, noise, etc) which lay outside of the scope of this consultation and report."

articles.body: The US attorney’s office in Washington has urged a federal judge to dismiss requests to unseal the search warrant used by federal agents to search Democratic Representative Ilhan Omar’s home earlier this month, arguing that releasing the records before the investigation is complete could jeopardise the proceedings.According to The New York Times, US Attorney Jeanine Pirro made the request in a 47-page court filing on Tuesday, saying the government did not necessarily oppose releasing some of the material later, subject to redactions. However, she described unsealing the records at this stage as “rash”, arguing that the investigation should be allowed to proceed until prosecutors decide whether to bring charges and make that decision public.Pirro also asked the court to give the government sufficient time to file an emergency motion seeking to block the release if the judge decides that unsealing the warrant is appropriate.Federal agents searched Omar’s Washington home on October 12, but the precise focus of the investigation has not been publicly established. Pirro has said her office is examining the lawmaker’s financial disclosures, while President Donald Trump has accused her of immigration fraud. Omar has denied wrongdoing and described the investigation as an attempt at political intimidation.Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin recently referred to an ongoing criminal investigation that could involve alleged fraud in the immigration paperwork of Omar’s family. Vice President JD Vance has also previously accused the congresswoman of immigration fraud, allegations she has rejected.Omar criticised the search on X, describing it as an attempt to target political opponents and weaponise federal law enforcement. Federal agents reportedly seized 17 items from her home, including phones and notebooks.The request to unseal the records was submitted by The New York Times and 14 other news organisations seeking greater transparency about the search and the reasons behind the investigation.The search took place weeks before Election Day, raising questions about the timing of the investigation. The Justice Department has historically sought to avoid actions that could influence elections during the 60 days before voting, although the application of that practice depends on the circumstances.Omar is seeking re-election to represent Minnesota’s 5th Congressional District, which includes Minneapolis and surrounding communities.You use AI every day. articles.title: West Virginia passed a law in 2021 after a federal judge's son was murdered; five years later a US appeals court struck down its ban on publishing judges' and police officers' home addresses without a notice safeguard
articles.summary: A federal appeals court in the United States has struck down a West Virginia privacy law.
articles.body: A federal appeals court in the United States has struck down a West Virginia privacy law. The law banned the publication of home addresses and personal details of judges, police officers and public officials. The court ruled that the law breaks the First Amendment of the US Constitution. A three-judge panel of the 4th US Circuit Court of Appeals in Richmond, Virginia, made the decision. It backed a lower district court ruling. That ruling found the state law placed an unconstitutional limit on the free flow of truthful, publicly available information. West Virginia lawmakers first passed the measure in 2021. They joined several other American states in passing laws known together as Daniel’s Law. The push across the country followed a tragedy in New Jersey in July 2020. Daniel Anderl, the 20-year-old son of US District Judge Esther Salas, was shot dead at the family home. The attacker was an angry attorney who had found the judge’s home address online. The appeals court agreed that the state has a strong interest in protecting public servants and their families from physical harm and harassment. But it said West Virginia’s law went too far. It made it a crime, and set penalties, for sharing address data. It did not include needed safeguards or a written notice requirement.Statutory flaws and First Amendment conflictsCircuit Judge Steven Agee wrote for the panel. He noted that state governments have a real duty to protect judges and police. But he said any law meant to do that must be narrowly written so it does not limit speech the Constitution protects. “This decision does not place information businesses beyond legitimate privacy regulation,” the court noted. It added that the outcome only restates that governments must respect First Amendment rights, even when they pursue the most compelling goals. Trade groups from the technology and data industries brought the lawsuit, including the Software and Information Industry Association. The plaintiffs argued that the West Virginia law put broad legal risk on data aggregators, news outlets and groups that compile public records. They said it gave affected people no first notice and no way to opt out. Under the West Virginia law that was struck down, a person could be sued and face set damages for showing or publishing covered personal information online. This applied even if the individual had never sent a written request to remove their details. Lawyers for the industry trade groups argued during oral arguments that without a required notice step, businesses and journalists faced strict liability. They said this covered the routine publishing or sharing of public records, such as property deeds, voter registrations and court filings, which naturally include address information.Differences across state privacy statutesThe 4th Circuit panel pointed out that West Virginia’s law was very different from similar privacy laws in other places, such as New Jersey. In New Jersey, the state Supreme Court upheld its version of Daniel’s Law. It found that legal liability began only after a person sent a formal written request asking that their personal information be taken down from public websites. By contrast, the West Virginia law did not have a standard rule that covered officials must first give notice to publishers or data handlers before liability or penalties could be sought. The federal panel decided this missing safeguard made the ban on speech too broad. It said the law chilled the routine publication of public records by news organisations, legal research services and commercial data brokers. Circuit Judges Pamela Harris and Steven Agee, along with their panel colleague, concluded that the law was subject to strict constitutional review. They said this was because it regulated content based on who was named and what type of data was involved. The court found that West Virginia failed to show that a less restrictive option, such as a notice-and-takedown process, would not work to protect judges.Broader legal implications for data privacyThe ruling sets an important legal precedent in the ongoing clash between privacy protections for public officials and free speech protections for businesses and media groups in the United States. In recent years, dozens of states have considered or passed versions of Daniel’s Law. These laws aim to protect judges, prosecutors, police officers and corrections staff from targeted violence and doxxing. Industry groups welcomed the appeals court ruling. They said physical safety is the top concern, but state legislatures cannot broadly limit access to public records or penalise information businesses without clear notice rules. West Virginia state officials have not yet said whether they plan to appeal the 4th Circuit decision to the United States Supreme Court. They have also not said whether they will ask the full appeals court to rehear the case. Legal experts expect that West Virginia lawmakers may have to rewrite the law to include clear written notice and takedown rules if they want it to meet federal constitutional standards.You use AI every day.
