articles.summary: Mahjong has infiltrated college tailgates and coaching households, with Power-four head coaches secretly competing against their wives and families.
articles.body: It's not only college football that has been the focus of my attention over the past three months. It is also the new American pastime that has taken over the kitchen tables of Southern women and is making its way into tailgates on a weekly basis across the country. It's not a new recipe, or a new table design. Instead, it's Mahjong. A simple walk to Tiger Stadium on the campus of Louisiana State University during the opening weekend of the college football season certainly changed my outlook on the newest trend sweeping the the nation, one expensive set at a time. LSU IS READY TO PARTY: LANE KIFFIN’S DEBUT BRINGS FIREWORKS TO DEATH VALLEY AFTER REVIVAL-LIKE BUILDUP It started a few months earlier when I was first introduced to this game, thanks to a friend we'll just call "Sam" for the sake of keeping the wild world of Mahjong between the groups that play it. I wouldn’t want to give away any secrets, and I would learn over time that this was on the same level as men getting together for a night of poker. The one thing I did not expect to see while making my way into a college football game was four ladies sitting at a table within a tailgate playing this game while others around them were immersed in your normal pregame activities that included alcohol. Did I just stumble into a whole new world? What was it about this game that led to women, and men, finding themselves sitting at a table covered in a 'mat' playing with 'tiles' that were labeled differently and a rule pamphlet that was also used to stir up the same table of "craks," "bams" and "dots." Yes, those are different items used to play Mahjong, which I still have no idea how to play. Also, it had unbeknownst to me, the game had made its way to other tailgates across college football that included Ole Miss, Alabama and Indiana. Yes, I know for a fact it's being played at other tailgates across this country, even if I haven’t been able to see it firsthand just yet. And why were there so many different colors involved, or why did every playing surface look different? Turns out, I was on the cusp of being astonished at how much this was actually being played around college athletics. No, I'm not just talking about the wives of coaches who might get together on a weekly basis to discuss life while playing this game. A 'tile' game at a tailgate: I had no idea what I was getting into I still remember, three or so months ago, when "Sam" told me I'd be surprised to know how many men participate in Mahjong as a way to decompress. More on that later, with a coaching twist. Now, for full disclosure, I have yet to learn the intricate details of this game, nor have I sat down to play a round. And, I'm not just talking about a hand of "cards." These were elaborate get togethers, with women hosting game nights usually on a rotating basis, while some outings will take place in a local studio or room that could also be used as a storefront. COLLEGE FOOTBALL'S JERRY JONES? TEXAS TECH BOOSTER CODY CAMPBELL DEMANDS RETURN ON INVESTMENT This turned into an investigative mission to find out how deep this whole Mahjong craze goes. It just so happens that there are actual stores that sell "tiles," playing "mats," sets that include marketing agreements with the 'Grateful Dead'. Yes, the band. How would I know about this? I'm sure by now you are wondering why in the world a sports writer would become so fascinated by a game that is played a majority of the time by women. It probably helps that "Sam" is so into this game that I have been running at system overload for months now, even though I enjoy hearing about these game nights that can most certainly be competitive. So, what did I do? This particular weekend had me in Tuscaloosa, Alabama, not far from home. Besides my algorithm on social media steering me toward different social media pages thanks to my curiosity, I needed to see what all the fuss was about. One google search later I found myself taking a detour on the way to Bryant-Denny Stadium to the Tuscaloosa Mahjong Parlor, just off the boulevard near the University of Alabama campus. The nerves I felt walking into this store were almost as intense as interviewing a head coach following a game, wondering where my brain would take me in the press conference setting. Luckily, Heather Fikes welcomed me into her store that is also home to a business ran by her husband, Steve, like I was just another friend on a random Friday afternoon. The colors were something I had never seen before, with boxes of "sets" stacked eloquently throughout the store. There were also 'mats', travel cases and just about anything else one could imagine needed for such a hobby. The awkward introduction by myself as a sports reporter looking to learn more about this game turned into a 45-minute conversation on nearly every single item for sale in this beautiful area designed just to sell the game known as "Mahjong." And no, sorry guys, this hobby is not cheap. I had to do a double-take when I heard that the colorful "Grateful Dead" set that caught my eye would cost over $400, which I immediately texted "Sam" about in full disbelief. Not because it wasn’t worth it, but more so at how shocked I was to learn how this game had taken on a life of itself over the years, at least in the deep south, and if I get caught in the storm it can be pricey. But don't worry, guys there's a cheaper way. I also didn’t know you could have a Mahjong "hookup" that could get you the same looking game equipment, but for a much cheaper price on what I would normally call the 'black market'. It was also Heather's husband, Steve, that reaffirmed my thoughts that this game was essentially the same as poker is for men. A way for women to gather within their communities to either let off some steam, congregate to share details of their life, or actually get into the competitive spirit. Yes, this can also get confrontational at times, with words being traded and attitudes checked at either the tailgate tent or the door to each hosting house. Turns out, this was more relevant than I had imagined, and not just outside the college football stadium in this case. Bringing the competition home, after a long day around the football facility For the sake of not giving other coaches ammunition to use within the group texts within the community of each conference, I decided to hold-off on actually naming the coaches who were drawn into this game by their wives or significant others. Also, there were coaches from six different conferences polled, so it would be hard to pin down a specific school. Thanks to "Sam" giving me the idea, along with a few sources with insider knowledge, I started randomly communicating with a number of college football head coaches to gauge whether they had been pulled into this lifestyle. "Dude, who told you I was playing?" one Power Four head coach responded to my question on whether they had ever played. "I use it as a way to relax, but unfortunately this damn game is addicting. I get home from the office and play a few rounds with my girls and wife. "But man, I thought we were competitive on the football field. This is a whole different animal. I did win a round last month, though." Then, it was another message to an unsuspecting coach within another conference. "Alright, who gave me up? That's some bulls—," another Power Four coach jokingly replied. "Yea Trey, I probably play at least once every two weeks. When you sit down at the table, and you have all of those darn tiles, I was lost for the first couple weeks. "I've got my wife over here talking smack, and then I'm getting it from my sister. Then, if I come home and she has friends over, I like to get at least one game in before heading upstairs. Every now and then I'm allowed to sit for a few rounds until it's time for me to leave the room so they can continue their night. If you're going to play, you better lock in, because they don't cut you any slack after a few practice rounds." For full transparency, I sent inquiries to ten different head coaches over a two-day period asking if they had ever played Mahjong. "I'm so confused most of the time, but it also gives me something that allows me to spend some extra time with my daughters," another head coach told OutKick. "So, if I get an extra hour a week with them over this game, I'll one day figure out a way to beat them. "They don't know it yet, but I've been watching tutorials online." articles.title: Why Arab parties may not be the ‘kingmakers’ in this Israeli election
articles.summary: Exit poll projections show that if Eisenkot’s bloc teamed up with Arab parties, they could potentially unseat Bibi.
articles.body:
Israel’s Arab-led parties are projected to win a record number of seats in the Israeli parliament, exit polls indicate, making them increasingly hard to ignore by the leading blocs.

“Probably the most important phenomenon of this election is the rise and the revival of the Arab vote,” Daniel Shek, a former Israeli ambassador, said. “The statement is clear: You cannot disregard such a large portion of the electorate in the calculations for Israeli politics.”

The latest projections from Tuesday’s voting showed that the Arab parties – the Joint List and Ra’am – could hold a record combined 17 seats in the 120-member Knesset.

So far, no clear winner has emerged as partial results give Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc 54 seats and the opposition alliance led by Gadi Eisenkot 49.

While Arab parties might theoretically wield influence as the two main blocs fail to win majorities in the Knesset, they are not “kingmakers”, observers said, pointing to what amounts to a political veto that limits Arab parties’ ability to turn electoral gains into influence.

“This veto is rooted in a racist structure that regards the Arab citizen as illegitimate and as an unwanted partner,” Honaida Ghanam, director general of the Palestinian Forum for Israeli Studies in Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, told Al Jazeera, alluding to the resistance by the majority of Israeli parties to form any government with Arab-led lists.

Both Netanyahu and Eisenkot have rejected the idea of partnering with them, citing a lack of shared values.

The numbers from exit poll projections thus far are looking clear: If Eisenkot’s bloc teams up with Arab parties, they could secure the 61 seats needed for a majority in parliament and depose Netanyahu.

According to The Times of Israel, the latest partial results would give a partnership between Eisenkot’s opposition alliance and Arab-led parties 66 seats.

According to Palestinian political analyst Ahmed Najar, the unwillingness by the opposition bloc to join forces is purely “ideological”.

“Eisenkot has imposed loyalty tests on Arab parties and ruled out relying on them even as the electoral arithmetic makes their support indispensable,” Najar told Al Jazeera.

How politically feasible is such a partnership?

According to Najar, a partnership with the Arab parties is not only feasible, it may be the only “realistic” route for Eisenkot to remove Netanyahu.

Omar Shaban, director of Palthink for Strategic Studies, pointed to the fact that Mansour Abbas, the leader of Ra’am, has already shown a willingness to join Eisenkot’s government if the Israeli candidate is elected, based on the condition that internal security matters will be handled by the Arab party.

Abbas has even appointed Jewish lawmaker Yoav Segalovitz to the number two spot on Ra’am’s electoral slate for the elections, Shaban explained.

Such a collaboration, if it came to fruition, could help foster better relations between Palestinian citizens and Jewish Israelis, he said.

Meanwhile, on Wednesday, Joint List leader Yousef Jabareen said his party is prepared to take responsibility for bringing Netanyahu’s far-right coalition down.

“The government has made the lives of every Arab citizen miserable,” Jabareen was quoted by the Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper as saying.

His movement “will know how to leverage” its political strength to advance its values, he added.

Ahmad Tibi, also a Joint List leader, on Wednesday said the bloc was extending its hand to the opposition alliance to oust Netanyahu, according to Israeli media reports. It was far from clear, however, that the bloc would formally join a governing coalition.

A roadblock to such a partnership is the more “radical” elements in Israeli society that Eisenkot would have to face who “don’t want the Israeli government to be supported or dependent on Arab votes”, Shabaan said.

Najar said Eisenkot would also have to persuade his prospective partners, including Naftali Bennett from the Together alliance and Avigdor Liberman, who heads the Yisrael Beytenu party.

“Politically, however, it would require him and his prospective partners, particularly Bennett and Lieberman, to abandon the longstanding Zionist consensus that Palestinian citizens of Israel may vote but that the parties representing them are not legitimate partners in governing the country,” he said.

Ghanam outlined four possible outcomes: another election, an opposition minority government supported from outside by Arab parties, defections from the opposition to Netanyahu’s bloc or a national unity government.

“Beyond the arithmetic, the most telling result of this election is the resilience of Netanyahu’s camp, which has proven deeply entrenched and cohesive,” she added.

What are the terms Eisenkot has laid out for a partnership with Arab parties?

According to The Times of Israel, Eisenkot has said he would consider partnering with any party that recognises Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, endorses the values of the Declaration of Independence and commits to all Israelis performing national service.

He hasn’t, however, expressed whether Ra’am, with or without Jewish lawmaker Segalovitz, would meet those criteria, the outlet also reported.

Have Jewish and Arab parties teamed up before?

Yes, there is precedent for such a move.

Most recently, after the 2021 elections, Ra’am emerged as a possible kingmaker, and its support was vital for the formation of the short-lived Bennett-Yair Lapid government at the time.

“Ra’am participated in the 2021-2022 coalition while Arab parties have previously supported governments from outside, most notably during the Rabin period,” Najar said, referring to Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin, who served in the country’s top post in the 1970s and 1990s.

“The obstacle is, therefore, neither constitutional nor practical but ideological.”

What have other party leaders said about partnering?

Netanyahu said on Tuesday that a coalition with Arab-led parties to form a government would be “a shame and a disgrace”.

“It is forbidden – simply forbidden – to endanger Israel and to establish a government that relies on anti-Zionist Arab parties,” he told supporters.

Bennett, meanwhile, who is currently in third place, has reversed course from the past: He has made clear that he now only wants “Zionist” parties in government and wants to exclude Arab parties.

By contrast, Yair Golan, leader of the centre-left Democrats party, which is part of the opposition bloc led by Eisenkot, has urged his allies to abandon their refusal to cooperate with Arab parties.

“We must no longer accept Netanyahu’s racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes,” Golan wrote on X.

What does the reluctance to partner say about Israeli democracy?

The reluctance of Jewish-led opposition parties to work with Arab parties “reveals the fundamentally racist structure of the Israeli political system”, Najar said.

“Jewish opposition leaders describe Netanyahu and the far right as an existential danger to democracy, yet many would apparently prefer Netanyahu to remain in power rather than share political power with Palestinian citizens of Israel,” he said.

Their objection is not only to a particular Arab party or programme but to the very idea that Palestinian representatives could possess genuine governing power, Najar added.

“A state cannot credibly call itself democratic when more than one-fifth of its citizens are permitted to vote but the representatives they elect are treated as inherently illegitimate,” he said.

Palestinian citizens of Israel, he pointed out, are accepted as voters when their participation serves the system but rejected as political actors when they seek the power to shape it, Najar added.

“This is not an accidental failure of Israeli democracy; it is the consequence of a system built to preserve Jewish political supremacy,” Najar said.

“If Eisenkot is serious about replacing Netanyahu, he must decide whether he is prepared to challenge that racist political order or remain confined by the same exclusionary logic that Netanyahu has spent years exploiting.”

articles.title: How could Israel break political deadlock? Here are four scenarios
articles.summary: With 85% of votes counted, all signs point to an impasse. The most likely outcome may be new elections.
articles.body:
Israel looks to be in political deadlock.

With 85% of votes counted after Tuesday's election, neither the incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition, nor the bloc of his key challenger Gadi Eisenkot look set to have a majority.

In order to form a government, it looks likely one of the leading parties would have to break their campaign promises - meaning the most probable outcome may well be new elections.

National unity government led by Netanyahu

Could Netanyahu persuade Eisenkot to join him in a national unity government?

Eisenkot would have to abandon his key platform to do so. He's framed himself as the only alternative to Netanyahu, and built his campaign on ousting him from power.

Just last night, he took to the stage at his campaign HQ and called on Netanyahu to "announce his retirement from political life today," telling the crowd that Israelis are fed up with Netanyahu's "culture of lies", "division and incitement".

But that was before one of the main exit polls - which had initially projected a lead for Eisenkot's bloc - was revised, and he was overtaken by Netanyahu.

Netanyahu could try to persuade Eisenkot's Yashar Party to join his Likud Party in a unity government by ditching the far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties he is currently in coalition with. But last night at Likud HQ he thanked his "loyal partners" and called for a "strong right-wing government"- remarks some have interpreted as meaning he intends to preserve his alliance with them.

One thing that could make a unity government more likely is a renewed conflict with Iran, which could place serious pressure on party leaders to put aside their political differences and work together. In the days prior to the election, Israeli and US media reported that Netanyahu was pushing for fresh strikes on the country, and had pressed Donald Trump to approve US involvement.

This would no-doubt be framed by Netanyahu's critics as an attempt to save his own political skin by entering another regional conflict.

Eisenkot-led coalition with Arab parties

This would be a seismic shift for Israeli politics. Only one independent Arab party has ever formally been part of a coalition, in 2021, and it didn't last long.

Eisenkot and every other Jewish party in his bloc bar one have already ruled out entering government with them. But right now, it's the opposition's only path to a majority.

The Arab parties were the story of election night. They look to have defied expectations and could gain a record 19 seats - helped by an unprecedented turnout from Israel's Arab population, who account for about one-fifth of the country and often describe themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel.

For years, many boycotted Israeli elections, saying voting would legitimise a system that they say treats them as second-class citizens. But their turnout last night, inspired by a desire to oust the most right-wing governing coalition in Israel's history, has shaken things up.

The United Arab list, who are currently projected to win around 7 seats, have said they'd join an opposition government, while The Joint List, who are projected to win 12 seats, have said they'd support one from outside.

However, the only Jewish leader advocating this scenario right now is The Democrats' Yair Golan. And a coalition like this would be very fragile, especially on issues like Gaza and the occupied West Bank.

The fact there is such a unified front from the Jewish parties against Arab participation points to Israel's deep divisions.

Netanyahu-led majority, with right-wingers from opposition

Could Netanyahu persuade the right-wing parties in Eisenkot's bloc to break away and join his coalition?

The two most likely candidates for this are Naftali Bennett - joint-leader of the Beyachad political alliance - and Avigdor Lieberman, leader of the Yisrael Beiteinu party. They are both right-wingers who are hardline on security, and share some political ground with Netanyahu.

But both campaigned explicitly to oust him, and to extend military conscription to the ultra-Orthodox - bringing them into direct conflict with the two ultra-Orthodox parties already part of Netanyahu's government. So it's difficult to see them joining forces.

Some have suggested Bennett and Lieberman's parties could replace the ultra-Orthodox parties, but current electoral math suggests that grouping may not have the seats needed for a majority.

If none of the above scenarios can be negotiated, the default outcome would be new elections.

Many would see this as a tacit win for Netanyahu, who would remain as caretaker PM until the new elections take place - which he may believe he has a better chance of winning.

Some analysts think the high Arab turnout would not be replicated again - especially if their record representation in parliament led to no change - and it could also mobilise more right-wing voters in a second poll. Netanyahu may also bet that the estimated 70,000 Israelis who flew home from abroad to vote, and are thought to skew against him, wouldn't do so again.

Additionally, several right-wing parties who failed to pass the electoral threshold of 3.25% may attract fewer votes or may not even run, thereby bringing more votes to Likud and its allies.

Between 2019 and 2022, Israel held five separate elections as Netanyahu and his rivals struggled time and again to co-operate.

articles.title: From Brazil to Cuba, US turns up the heat
articles.summary: TOI Correspondent from Washington: US President Donald Trump's campaign to assert American primacy in the western hemisphere produced fireworks on two
articles.body: TOI Correspondent from Washington: US President Donald Trump's campaign to assert American primacy in the western hemisphere produced fireworks on two fronts on Wednesday. First Washington gave refuge to defeated Brazilian presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro as he fled the country; then it expelled from the US a Cuban diplomat alleging he tried to assault an American official. The twin episodes, coming amid the US overhang on elections in Israel and Serbia, raised questions about the use of American power and influence across the world, and its international obligations.The immediate flashpoint was Brazil, Latin America’s largest country, where the announcement by the State Department on Tuesday that Flavio Bolsonaro and his family would receive US visas after his loss to incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in Sunday’s presidential runoff triggered an uproar. Bolsonaro was reported to have been spirited out of Brazil even as Brazilian law-enforcement was closing in on him after a Court order requiring him to surrender his passports took effect, amid investigations into alleged financial wrongdoing that he denies.Bolsonaro, a senator and the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, lost after campaigning on a promise to secure his father’s release. The elder Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest for attempting to overturn the 2022 election result, echoing the 2020 insurrection in the US Flavio too has refused to concede defeat and alleged electoral irregularities in the just concluded election without producing evidence sufficient to substantiate his claims.For Lula's government, the visa decision will be difficult to separate from Washington’s broader pattern of pressure on Brasília. Trump too has questioned Brazil’s electoral process, imposed tariffs on Brazilian exports and supported the Bolsonaro family’s political cause.Washington also revoked the visa of Brazil’s ambassador in August amid a dispute over diplomatic appointments and access for US officials. Brasília has characterised such measures as politically motivated interference in its domestic affairs. A Brazilian judge on Tuesday ordered a police investigation into alleged ties between a donor network co-founded by Vice President JD Vance and the Bolsonaro campaign.While the distinction between granting entry and offering political protection is important -- a US visa does not confer asylum, immunity from prosecution or permanent refuge -- the political signal is unmistakable. By welcoming a defeated opposition leader facing domestic legal scrutiny, Washington risks reinforcing perceptions that its support for democratic processes is conditional on whether the winners are ideologically aligned.The precedent is not without historical parallels. In 1979, President Jimmy Carter admitted the ailing Shah of Iran, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, for medical treatment after the Islamic Revolution had driven him into exile. Iranian revolutionaries cited the decision as justification for seizing the US Embassy in Tehran, beginning a 444-day hostage crisis that transformed relations between Washington and Tehran for generations. The episode became a potent symbol of American interference and the perceived protection of a discredited ally.The point, diplomats say, is not that sheltering a foreign political figure inevitably produces disaster. Governments, including New Delhi, often admit exiles, dissidents and former allies for humanitarian, political or strategic reasons. But decisions framed in Washington or New Delhi as individual concerns can acquire a very different meaning in the country from which the individual has fled as is happening in Brazil and Bangladesh.In a separate flare-up, US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz and Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez engaged in an extraordinary slanging match during a General Assembly debate over Washington’s decades-old economic embargo against Cuba. Cuban delegates banged on their table and shouted objections as Waltz denounced Havana, holding up a photos of Cuban leaders, including the late Fidel Castro wearing Rolex watches. Rodriguez approached the podium and called the American ambassador a liar. “This is America. Back up,” Waltz retorted as the fracas intensified. Observers later pointed out that while the US hosts the United Nations, it is not an American institution and Washington does not have sovereign authority over the organisation.Still, the First Secretary of Cuba's UN delegation Richard Tur de la Concepcion was sent packing back to Havana with accusations that during the altercation, he lunged at Waltz's spokesman, JP Freire, and attempted to snatch an iPhone Freire was recording with. "You lay a hand on an American here in the United States,... we're not gonna stand for it," Waltz later said, revealing that Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is Cuban-American, has signed paperwork to expel Conception.You use AI every day. articles.title: Scientists analysed 640 charcoal fragments from a Spanish rock shelter and found Neanderthals may have organised different areas around ancient fireplaces
articles.summary: Charcoal remains from a Spanish rock shelter are offering clues to how Neanderthals organised their living spaces.
articles.body: Charcoal remains from a Spanish rock shelter are offering clues to how Neanderthals organised their living spaces. Researchers examined 640 charcoal fragments from level Ra at Abric Romaní, a site near Capellades in Barcelona. Their analysis found a concentration of charcoal around hearths in the northern sector, while the southern sector contained smaller and more isolated patches.According to research published in the Journal of Paleolithic Archaeology titled “The Use of Space in Neanderthal Campsites: Evidence from Spatial and Taphonomic Analyses of Charcoal Remains from Level Ra of Abric Romaní (Barcelona, Spain)”, the charcoal fragments were concentrated around hearths in the northern section, while the southern section contained smaller, more scattered accumulations.Charcoal fragments reveal differences in Neanderthal activity around fireplacesThe researchers mapped charcoal fragments recovered during excavations from 2019 to 2022 and compared their locations with hearths and signs of natural alteration. The northern sector contained 495 fragments, many in broad concentrations overlapping with hearths near the shelter wall. The southern sector held 145 fragments in smaller, more isolated patches with less consistent overlap with hearths.The team used spatial analysis to examine whether these differences reflected human activity or later natural movement. After accounting for signs of water-related alteration, the distribution still suggested different uses of the two areas.Wood fragments offer clues about Neanderthal fuel collectionWood identification showed that mountain pine accounted for about 75% of the charcoal record. The researchers grouped several mountain pine species because their wood anatomy makes them difficult to distinguish. They noted that Neanderthals probably collected fuelwood from the area around the shelter, where pine was abundant.The charcoal’s condition was consistent with deadwood in varying states of decay, probably including many branches. Compression wood was common, a feature that can occur in branches as well as in trees growing under stress. The team said further analysis would be needed to distinguish branches from trunks more clearly.Water-related changes affected charcoal remains across the shelterThe charcoal had also been affected by natural processes after it was deposited. Researchers identified mineral concretions and other changes linked to water carrying dissolved minerals through the shelter. These alterations were proportionally more common among fragments from the southern sector, complicating the interpretation of its smaller charcoal patches, although the northern squares, near the wall, had higher absolute counts of altered fragments.The study found that water-related processes affected specific parts of the site, but overall post-depositional disturbance was low to moderate. The team considered human activity the main influence on the charcoal’s distribution, while acknowledging that natural processes could explain some patterns.What do the charcoal remains reveal about ancient activity at the shelterAccording to the researchers, the southern charcoal patches may indicate discrete hearth-cleaning events, during which burned remains were moved a short distance away from fireplaces.They also considered whether the deposits formed during separate visits, with later groups reusing existing hearths. The charcoal alone cannot distinguish between these possibilities. The team recommended studying the distribution of stone tools, bones, and sediments alongside the hearths to build a picture of activity at the shelter. Such evidence could help establish whether charcoal was displaced in one occupation or accumulated across several.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: At least 68 dead in Spain's second major train crash this year
articles.summary: URDA, Spain, Oct 28 (Reuters) - At least 68 people died when two Spanish high-speed trains collided on Wednesday, with rescuers scouring the wreckage for mor...
articles.body:
Collision of two high-speed trains between the towns of Mora and Orgaz

By David Latona, Guillermo Martinez and Michael Francis Gore

URDA, Spain, Oct 28 (Reuters) - At least 68 people died when two Spanish high-speed trains collided on Wednesday, with rescuers scouring the wreckage for more bodies after Spain's second deadly rail accident this year and Europe's deadliest since 2013.

Spain's transport minister said Wednesday's crash south of Madrid occurred after a Renfe train was authorised to continue its journey despite ‌there being an active red signal because of a stationary train on the track ahead.

Oscar Puente told reporters in Madrid that the red signal was issued due to a computer communications failure, which automatically stopped ‌traffic, and an erroneous decision had been made to restart the Renfe train, in a breach of protocol.

Ambulances, funeral home vans and helicopters were parked next to one of the trains on an elevated section of track, while twisted metal, broken panels and wreckage were strewn across an embankment down ​which at least three carriages had plunged.

Evacuated passengers streamed along a nearby road. Some were splattered with blood or had bandaged wounds, while others wheeled suitcases and were handed water by volunteers.

Miguel, who was travelling with several colleagues in the rear carriage of one of the trains, described the moment of the accident and its immediate aftermath.

"We heard a massive roar, a truly enormous thud that went on for 10 seconds, as if the train were about to derail. Through the right-hand window, we could see a wrecked train," he told COPE radio.

The head of Castilla-La Mancha's regional government said the death toll had risen to 68, while rescue workers were still going carriage by carriage looking for other crash victims.

OPERATOR RENFE SAYS CIRCUMSTANCES ‌BEING INVESTIGATED

The collision comes after an accident in January between high-speed trains belonging to ⁠the same operators and on the same line that killed 46 people.

In that crash a train derailed and smashed into an oncoming train near Adamuz, in Cordoba province, prompting a debate about the level of investment in railway maintenance in recent years.

A person briefed on Wednesday's disaster said a train operated by private consortium Iryo stopped near Toledo on orders from infrastructure manager ⁠Adif due to a signal fault.

A train operated by Renfe then struck the stationary train at high speed, causing several carriages of both trains to derail, the person said.

Renfe said in a statement that after being authorised to continue its journey, its train had crashed into the Iryo train that had remained stationary "for reasons we don't know".

"The Renfe train continued on its way as instructed, and a collision occurred. The exact sequence of events, the traffic conditions and the circumstances of the impact will have to be established by the ​investigation," ​Renfe said.

There was no immediate response to a Reuters request for comment from Iryo or Adif.

Authorities gave no immediate ​figure for the number of injured but Health Minister Mónica García urged people in a ‌post on X to donate blood. Castilla-La Mancha region spokesperson Esther Padilla said 147 people had been travelling on the Iryo train and 397 on the Renfe train.

The accident is the deadliest in Europe since a 2013 crash in Spain's Santiago de Compostela left 80 people dead.

Eduarda, a passenger on the Iryo train, told Cadena SER radio she felt a strong impact that threw her forward, initially making her think the train had made an emergency stop.

She only realised the seriousness of the accident after seeing injured people and being told to evacuate.

After climbing down an embankment to safety, she saw what she described as a catastrophic scene, with part of the train hanging down the slope and a fire in one carriage.

Emergency responders, including a helicopter, police and ambulances, arrived within about 20 minutes, she said. "I saw dead people," she said.

The Renfe and Iryo trains crashed just after 9 a.m., causing two Iryo wagons to derail, a spokesperson for the Castilla-La Mancha region ‌said.

Renfe said it had activated a special line for families of victims and expressed its condolences. Iryo said it had activated emergency ​protocols.

The causes of the January accident near Cordoba are still under investigation. A preliminary report by Spain's Civil Guard in February pointed to defects ​in the track, rail or weld between two sections of track as the main hypothesis for the accident, ​but kept seven other theories open.

The latest accident comes as Spain gears up for an election on November 29. Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez was on his way to the ‌scene of the crash, his office said. The opposition People's Party cancelled all campaign events, ​a spokesperson said.

"Shocked by the serious train accident in Toledo. ​My affection, solidarity, and support to all the victims and their families," Sanchez said on X.

Accidents, including derailments and collisions, increased from 45 in 2016 to 57 in 2024 and 69 last year, according to Spain's railway safety authority.

Some 25 million passengers used a high-speed train in Spain in the first half of the year, a decline of roughly 14% compared with the same period last year, according to a Reuters analysis of data ​from Spain's competition authority.

European Commission data shows Spain's maintenance investment in its roughly 4,000 ‌km (2,485 miles) of high-speed lines has lagged large European peers, despite an unmatched drive to expand the network.

Spain spent an average of about €1.5 billion a year from 2018 to 2022 on its high-speed network, ​more than any other country. The vast majority went to new infrastructure with only some 16% earmarked for maintenance, renewal and upgrades.

(Reporting by David Latona, Emma Pinedo, Mireia Merino, Corina Pons, Victoria Waldersee, Benjamin ​Mejias, Joan Faus and Pietro Lombardi; Writing by Charlie Devereux and Alexander Smith; Editing by Toby Chopra and Alison Williams)

articles.title: After donating blood to an injured colleague in 1998, Bengal road worker Toran Sheikh kept helping strangers; 28 years later, the daily-wage labourer has donated blood 105 times and runs village camps
articles.summary: Toran Sheikh is a daily-wage labourer and road worker from West Bengal. One day he decided to donate blood to a needy person purely out of humanity.
articles.body: Toran Sheikh is a daily-wage labourer and road worker from West Bengal. One day he decided to donate blood to a needy person purely out of humanity. He had no grand ambition to change the world. It began with an injured colleague who desperately needed help. In 1998, when a fellow worker suffered a serious road accident, Sheikh donated blood to him as it was much-needed to save his friend’s life.Almost 30 years later, Sheikh from Khalipur village in Purba Bardhaman district, has donated blood 105 times. He has also worked to encourage others to do the same and organised blood-donation camps in remote villages.His incredible journey, as reported by The New Indian Express, is a reminder that the desire to help others does not depend on wealth or social standing.An accident that changed his lifeSheikh first donated blood when he was only 18. His colleague, who worked alongside him, was injured in an accident. He was in need of blood urgently. Sheikh donated blood and helped his friend. The experience left a lasting impression on him. He realised how something as simple as donating blood could make the difference between life and death.“There is no justification to verify the identity of a distressed person in terms of religion, cast and creed. No difference in colour and religion should be taken into account when someone cries for blood,” Sheikh told The New Indian Express.A daily-wage worker who refuses to give upSheikh's commitment is quite inspiring. Now 50, he works repairing roads across Purba Bardhaman, Paschim Bardhaman and parts of Murshidabad. Employed by contractors working with local administrations, he earns approximately Rs 700-800 a day.He supports his wife, two daughters and son with this income. The family lives in a mud house, and their financial situation becomes more difficult during the monsoon.To supplement his earnings, Sheikh also supplies labourers to contractors in Khalipur and Bamundi. Yet, he continues to devote time to blood donation and community awareness.Taking the message to remote villagesSheikh has also established the Katwa Sub-division Voluntary Blood Donation Forum to organise donation camps in remote villages and motivate residents to participate. His work extends to tribal-dominated areas of Bardhaman.His message is also printed on his business card, which says, “Swechhaay rakto dan karun/manuser mangal korun,” which is an appeal to donate blood voluntarily and work for the good of humanity.Not only this, every year, on World Blood Donor Day on June 14, state government blood banks invite him to speak about voluntary blood donation. This year at the Government Institute of Blood Transfusion Medicine and Immuno Haematology, commonly known as the Central Blood Bank, he brought tribal residents from Ambal village in Purba Bardhaman's Ketugram II block to donate blood voluntarily.A donation that stood out during CovidAccording to Bengali newspaper Sangbad Pratidin, during the Covid-19 lockdown, an 86-year-old woman named Shobharani Talukdar, a resident of Katwa's Panuhat, urgently needed blood.Her family struggled to find a donor, and the blood bank reportedly had no blood available. But Sheikh reached Katwa Hospital and donated blood to help her.Recognition for a lifetime of serviceOn October 1, 2026, West Bengal's Health Minister, Dr Sharadwat Mukherjee, felicitated Sheikh at Swasthya Bhawan in Salt Lake, recognising both his repeated donations and his efforts to spread awareness among marginalised communities.By October 25, the newspaper reported that he had donated blood 105 times. An earlier report by Sangbad Pratidin, published on October 10, recorded 102 donations.His work offers a simple but powerful reminder of humanity is still alive and you don't have to be rich to be human and do service.You use AI every day. articles.title: Kremlin says European countries not included in next Ukraine talks
articles.summary: The comment comes as UK and Netherlands pledge extra military support for Kyiv.
articles.body:
European countries will not be included in the next round of talks with Ukraine and the United States planned to take place in Abu Dhabi, according to a top foreign policy aide at the Kremlin.

Interfax news agency quoted Yuri Ushakov, who said the possible participation of European countries was not discussed during a 90-minute phone call on Tuesday among Russian President Vladimir Putin, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store.

But Stubb offered a different account, telling a meeting of the Nordic Council in Helsinki that European countries would be involved in November’s Abu Dhabi talks.

Speaking at a news conference in the Netherlands on Wednesday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said trilateral talks with Russia and the US would take place from November 6 to November 10 in the United Arab Emirates.

Zelenskyy said Kyiv wanted Europe to also be involved in the talks, adding that unity and stronger pressure on Russia were needed.

His comments came after he met with Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten, who pledged an extra 500 million euros ($556m) for military support to Ukraine this winter to buy drones and other material to strengthen Ukraine’s defences. Zelenskyy is also due to meet Dutch King Willem-Alexander on Wednesday.

Earlier in the day before Zelenskyy’s visit, the Dutch government announced a new support package for Ukraine worth 1.2 billion euros ($1.33bn) over the next three years and a contribution of 40 million euros ($44.5m) by the end of this year to the Ukraine Energy Support Fund.

“Support for recovery and reconstruction can’t wait for a ceasefire. Ukraine needs our help right now – military support but also social and economic assistance,” Sjoerd Sjoerdsma, the Dutch minister for foreign trade and development cooperation, said during a visit to Kyiv on Wednesday.

“However successful you are on the battlefield, it’s also essential that energy systems, hospitals and food production keep ticking over,” he added.

In a separate development, Zelenskyy thanked British Prime Minister Andy Burnham for a newly announced additional support package worth 10 billion pounds ($13.3bn) after a Wednesday morning phone call.

“A truly strong and very timely step – coming right as Russia needs to see and feel that Ukraine will not be left alone to deal with the problems Russia is so eager to escalate,” Zelenskyy wrote on social media.

According to Downing Street , the new British aid package for Ukraine includes 500 million pounds ($665m) in additional military support from the Ministry of Defence “to plug urgent gaps in Ukraine’s air defences this winter”.
